name: A worried customer
situation: A hotel receptionist is helping an exhausted traveler who thought their reservation was lost. While checking, the receptionist has just found the prepaid reservation under a misspelled surname and confirmed the room is ready. They can now explain the mistake and offer a practical next step.
transcript:
Guest: I have been traveling all night. Please tell me I still have a room.
Receptionist: May I see your booking number?
Guest: Here. I am really worried. Your colleague said nothing was under my name.
Receptionist: I am checking the confirmation directly.
Guest: I cannot do another hotel tonight. What is happening?

name: A repeated interruption
situation: A tired colleague is interrupted for the fourth time about an answer they already sent. Their patience is wearing thin, but the other colleague has now admitted they fear giving a client the wrong number. The speaker needs to set a boundary, point to the exact answer in the email, and then help them handle their worry.
transcript:
Colleague: Did you check the number?
Speaker: I sent it ten minutes ago.
Colleague: Can you check it again?
Speaker: It is in the email, second paragraph, marked final.
Colleague: Just check one more time. I know I keep asking. I am scared I will give the client the wrong figure and get blamed again.

name: A new employee is unsure
situation: A new employee has been asked an unfamiliar technical question. They were unsure, but have now found the manufacturer compatibility sheet. It confirms this adapter supports the customer's two-display configuration at sixty hertz, but not at one hundred twenty hertz. They should acknowledge their earlier uncertainty, explain the verified limit, and help the customer decide.
transcript:
Customer: Does the adapter support that configuration?
Employee: I have not used that setup yet.
Customer: Could you confirm it before I buy it?
